questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: Why is the scheduled host unable to conduct the interview?

choices.A: The soundboard stops working.
choices.B: She has lost the question list.
choices.C: The baker arrives late.
choices.D: Her bus has stalled.

questions.correctAnswer: Her bus has stalled.
questions.explanation: The host messages Eli that her bus has stalled shortly before airtime.
questions.stimulusText:
Eli had volunteered to operate the soundboard for the school’s weekly radio program because the job seemed safely invisible. He adjusted music levels, watched the clock, and signaled the student hosts through a glass window. Speaking belonged to someone else.
On Friday, a local baker was scheduled for an interview about reducing food waste. Two minutes before airtime, the host sent a message saying her bus had stalled. The second host was already reading announcements in the studio. Eli could either cancel the interview or conduct it himself.
When the baker arrived, Eli opened the microphone and asked his first prepared question. Then he glanced at the next line too early and missed part of the response. Seven seconds of silence filled his headphones. Instead of rushing ahead, he asked, “What made that first experiment work?” The baker described turning day-old bread into crisp toppings, and the conversation began to flow.
After the broadcast, Eli apologized for the pause. The baker laughed. “I thought you were listening.” Eli replayed the recording. The silence no longer sounded like an empty space. It sounded like the moment he stopped hiding behind his list and became curious about the answer.

questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: What is recorded in an odor profile?

choices.A: Only the age and weight of the object
choices.B: Chemical findings and human descriptions
choices.C: A photograph of every trial mixture
choices.D: Instructions for touching the artifact

questions.correctAnswer: Chemical findings and human descriptions
questions.explanation: The passage states that an odor profile combines chemical findings with descriptions from volunteers.
questions.stimulusText:
Museums preserve objects that can be seen and touched, but some researchers also collect scents. Smell is part of the experience of places and materials, yet it is difficult to store. An old book, a wooden workshop, or a historic soap may lose its characteristic odor as its ingredients change over time.
To document a scent, researchers may place an object in a sealed container with a material that traps airborne molecules. Laboratory instruments then separate and identify many of those molecules. A written “odor profile” records both the chemical findings and descriptions supplied by human volunteers, such as smoky, grassy, or sweet.
Re-creating the scent is a separate challenge. A list of molecules does not automatically reveal the exact amounts needed, and people may describe the same odor differently. Researchers therefore compare several trial mixtures with the original object. They also avoid exposing fragile artifacts to substances that might damage them.
Scent archives can support conservation and education. If a material’s odor changes, that shift may provide evidence of decay. A carefully reconstructed scent can also help visitors imagine a setting without touching its original objects. Such collections do not replace visual records; they preserve another layer of information that would otherwise disappear.

questions.stimulusTitle: The Margin as a Meeting Place
questions.stimulusText:
Many readers are taught to keep library books free of marks, and for good reason. Yet in books people own, handwritten notes can reveal an active conversation between reader and text. A question beside a puzzling paragraph, a line connecting two ideas, or a brief disagreement records thought at the moment it occurs.
Marginal notes also allow a reader to meet an earlier version of oneself. A comment that once seemed insightful may later appear incomplete. Rather than proving the first reading was useless, the contrast shows that understanding has changed. The page becomes a record of revision, not just of information received.
Some notes face outward as well. Families sometimes pass books from one generation to another, and scholars study annotations in writers’ personal libraries. These marks can reveal which passages attracted attention or how an idea developed. Still, a note is evidence of one response, not a final explanation of what a passage means.
Digital reading tools can preserve comments without placing ink on paper. Whether written with pencil or typed on a screen, useful annotation does more than decorate a page. It identifies a connection, asks a focused question, or tests an interpretation. In this way, the margin becomes not an escape from the text but a place to engage with it.

questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: Why does the pale blue thread appear to match during the performance?

choices.A: The prince’s costume is entirely blue.
choices.B: The designer paints the thread silver.
choices.C: Blue stage lighting makes the thread less noticeable.
choices.D: The actor covers the repair with a cape.

questions.correctAnswer: Blue stage lighting makes the thread less noticeable.
questions.explanation: The stage’s blue lighting causes the pale blue thread to nearly disappear against the costume.
questions.stimulusText:
Minutes before the curtain rose, Nia discovered that the silver braid on the prince’s costume had pulled loose. As the student responsible for wardrobe repairs, she had packed needles, pins, and thread in several colors, but no silver. The costume designer was helping an actor in another room, and the braid continued to unravel.
Nia spotted a spool of pale blue thread in the sewing box. Under the workroom lights, it clearly did not match. She carried the spool beside the stage, where the scene’s blue lighting washed across the costume. Against that light, the thread nearly disappeared.
She made several small stitches instead of one long row, knotting each section separately. If one stitch broke, the others would still hold. The actor hurried onstage, and the repair survived a sword fight, a dance, and three quick costume changes.
After the show, the designer examined Nia’s work. Nia began explaining why she had used the wrong color. “It was the right color for where it had to work,” the designer said. She showed Nia how to replace it with silver for the next performance, but she left one blue stitch hidden beneath the braid as a reminder: a good solution depends not only on the materials available, but also on the conditions in which they will be seen.

questions.prompt: Which condition is commonly found in singing dunes?

choices.A: Wet grains of many different sizes
choices.B: Large stones mixed throughout the sand
choices.C: Dry grains that are similar in size
choices.D: Flat slopes protected from movement

questions.correctAnswer: Dry grains that are similar in size
questions.explanation: The passage identifies dry, similarly sized, smooth grains as common in singing dunes.
questions.stimulusText:
On a few dunes around the world, sliding sand can produce a deep hum that lasts for several seconds. The sound is sometimes called booming or singing sand. It does not occur whenever sand moves, and even nearby dunes may behave differently.
Researchers have found that grain properties matter. Singing dunes often contain dry, similarly sized grains with smooth surfaces. When a layer of these grains slides down a steep slope, many grains move in a coordinated way. Their repeated collisions create vibrations. The moving layer and the dune beneath it can reinforce particular frequencies, producing a sound much louder than separate grains would make.
Moisture can interrupt this process by changing how grains contact one another. Dust or a mixture of very different grain sizes may also prevent synchronized movement. Wind helps shape a dune and restore steep slopes, but wind alone does not create the booming sound.
Scientists still investigate how a dune’s size and internal layers affect its pitch. Measurements suggest that thicker moving layers tend to produce lower sounds. By comparing dunes, researchers can test how grain motion, slope, and dune structure combine to turn countless tiny impacts into one powerful tone.

questions.explanation: The moving layer and dune strengthen particular vibrations, making the sound louder.

questions.prompt: Why did signal systems use bold patterns?

choices.A: They remained visible through every kind of weather.
choices.B: They were cheaper to produce than plain flags.
choices.C: They showed how much cargo a ship carried.
choices.D: They could be recognized from a distance.

questions.correctAnswer: They could be recognized from a distance.
questions.explanation: Bold patterns made signals easier to distinguish from far away.
questions.stimulusText:
Before radios became standard on ships, busy harbors relied on visible signals to exchange information. Flags could identify a vessel, request assistance, or announce that cargo was ready. Because a flag’s meaning had to be recognized from far away, successful systems used bold patterns and limited sets of agreed-upon signals.
Weather created difficulties. Fog could hide a flag, while weak wind left it hanging unreadably. Harbors therefore combined methods. Signal stations might raise geometric shapes on a mast, ring bells, fire a harmless sound signal, or use lamps after dark. Each method worked under some conditions and failed under others.
Speed also mattered. A complicated message sent one flag at a time could delay a ship entering a narrow channel. Standard codes shortened common instructions. Instead of spelling an entire warning, one signal could tell a captain to wait while another vessel passed.
These systems required shared knowledge. Harbor workers maintained equipment, ships carried codebooks, and crews practiced recognizing signals. The flags and shapes were simple objects, but the communication network was not simple. It depended on preparation, agreement, and several backup methods working together.

questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: What happens when Mara points a narrow corner toward the breeze?

choices.A: Air moves around the lantern and the paper stops bending.
choices.B: The folded decorations tear away from the top.
choices.C: The cardboard panels become heavier.
choices.D: The lantern rotates back toward its broadest face.

questions.correctAnswer: Air moves around the lantern and the paper stops bending.
questions.explanation: Pointing a corner into the breeze allows air to flow around both sides and reduces pressure on a panel.
questions.stimulusText:
Mara’s class had built paper lanterns for the courtyard festival. Her lantern was a tall hexagon covered with thin green paper. In the classroom it stood perfectly, but outside, the first breeze pushed one side inward.
Mara’s first thought was to add heavier cardboard to every panel. Mr. Chen, the art teacher, asked her to carry the lantern across the courtyard before changing it. As she walked, Mara noticed that the wind struck the broadest face directly. When she turned the lantern so that one narrow corner faced the breeze, air moved around both sides and the paper stopped bending.
The display stands could not be rotated every time the wind shifted. Mara cut small openings beneath the folded decorations near the top and bottom. From a distance, the openings remained hidden, but they allowed trapped air to escape. She tested the lantern with a fan at three speeds and reinforced only the two joints that still flexed.
At the festival, the green paper trembled without collapsing. Mr. Chen asked whether the lantern was stronger. Mara considered the question. It contained very little additional material. “It is better at letting the wind pass,” she said. She had begun by trying to defeat the breeze and ended by designing a path for it.

choices.A: Two cream squares
choices.B: A red diamond and a circle

choices.D: Two complete blue triangles

questions.correctAnswer: A chipped blue square and a narrow blue fragment
questions.explanation: Jules pairs the chipped blue square with a narrow blue fragment to create a triangular outline.
questions.stimulusText:
Jules helped his grandfather arrange tiles for a small mosaic table. The design repeated a red diamond, two cream squares, and a blue triangle around the edge. Near the final corner, they discovered that the box contained no more blue triangles.
“We can order another,” Jules said, though the family picnic was the next morning. His grandfather spread the remaining pieces on a towel: circles, narrow rectangles, and one chipped blue square. None matched the missing tile.
Jules tried filling the space with a cream square, but the repeated pattern looked interrupted. Then he examined the chipped blue tile. He placed its broken edge against the table’s outer rim and paired it with a narrow blue fragment from the scrap jar. Together, the two pieces formed the outline of a triangle, though a thin seam crossed the middle.
Jules expected his grandfather to reject the visible seam. Instead, his grandfather placed a similar seam through each of the other blue triangles using slender cream strips. The repair no longer looked like an exception; it became a feature repeated throughout the border.
At the picnic, a cousin traced the cream lines and asked where the pattern had come from. Jules glanced at the once-chipped square. “From the piece we did not have,” he replied.

questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: What creates pressure that moves water through the pipe?

choices.A: Heat absorbed by the central structure
choices.B: An electric pump inside the tower
choices.C: A difference in elevation
choices.D: Wind striking the nozzle

questions.correctAnswer: A difference in elevation
questions.explanation: Water moving from a higher elevation creates pressure without an electric pump.
questions.stimulusText:
In high mountain regions, winter water may be plentiful while spring planting water is scarce. Snow and ice often melt too late or flow away before fields need irrigation. Some communities address this timing problem by building cone-shaped towers of ice during cold months.
Water from a stream or uphill pipe travels downward through a narrow pipe. The difference in elevation creates pressure, so no electric pump is required. A nozzle sprays the water into freezing air. Droplets freeze as they fall and gradually build a tall cone around a central structure.
The cone shape is useful because it exposes less surface area to sunlight than a shallow sheet holding the same amount of ice. As temperatures rise, the tower melts slowly. Channels carry the released water toward young trees or fields. Builders may adjust a tower’s location and size according to shade, wind, expected temperatures, and local water needs.
These ice towers do not increase the total amount of water in a watershed. Instead, they temporarily store part of a winter flow and release it later. Their success depends on sufficiently cold construction weather and careful placement. Where conditions fit, the towers serve as seasonal reservoirs built from the water they are designed to save.

questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: What causes the sensor’s unusually high reading?

choices.A: A sunbeam heats its black plastic case.
choices.B: The greenhouse heater turns on automatically.
choices.C: Ana places it beside a shaded thermometer.
choices.D: Rainwater enters its digital screen.

questions.correctAnswer: A sunbeam heats its black plastic case.
questions.explanation: Direct sunlight warms the sensor’s dark case, causing it to register local heat rather than general air temperature.
questions.stimulusText:
For the science club’s greenhouse project, Dev recorded the temperature every afternoon. The chart rose gently on sunny days and dipped after rain. Then Tuesday’s entry showed 119°F, even though the greenhouse had felt only pleasantly warm.
Dev’s partner, Ana, wanted to erase the number. “It is obviously wrong,” she said. Dev agreed that the greenhouse had not reached 119°F, but he drew a box around the entry instead. They checked the digital sensor and found its screen working normally.
The next afternoon, Dev watched the sensor at the usual recording time. A narrow beam of sunlight moved across the wall and struck the black plastic case. Within minutes, the displayed temperature climbed far above the reading from a shaded thermometer nearby. The sensor was measuring heat around its sun-warmed case rather than the greenhouse air.
Dev and Ana built a small white cover that shaded the device while allowing air to circulate. They kept Tuesday’s number on the chart and added a note explaining the problem. At the project fair, the unusual point attracted more questions than the smooth parts of the graph. Dev realized that a mistaken measurement could still be accurate evidence—just not evidence of what he had first assumed.

questions.stimulusTitle: The Flexible Armor of a Pangolin
questions.stimulusText:
A pangolin’s body is covered with overlapping scales made largely of keratin, the same type of protein found in human fingernails. The scales provide protection, but an animal covered by rigid plates must still be able to move.
The solution lies partly in arrangement. Each scale overlaps nearby scales like a roof tile, yet its base attaches to flexible skin. When the pangolin walks or climbs, the scales shift slightly over one another. When threatened, the animal curls into a ball. The scales spread at their exposed edges while continuing to cover the softer skin beneath them.
Shape also contributes to strength. A scale is not a flat sheet; it curves and contains layers of fibers oriented in different directions. A crack that begins in one layer may be redirected or slowed when it reaches another. This layered structure helps prevent a small defect from traveling straight through the scale.
Researchers study such biological structures for design ideas. Overlapping protective panels might be useful where equipment must resist impact without becoming completely stiff. Copying a scale exactly is not always necessary. Engineers may instead apply the broader principles: movable overlap, curved surfaces, and layered fibers that guide damage away from a direct path.

questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: What did arrows represent in Maris’s notation?

choices.A: Direction
choices.B: Duration
choices.C: Height
choices.D: A dancer’s name

questions.correctAnswer: Direction
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that arrows showed direction.
questions.stimulusText:
Choreographer Elena Maris often created dance sequences by demonstrating them in a studio. Dancers learned by watching and repeating. When a performer asked how an older work had originally ended, however, Maris discovered that memory and a grainy video offered different answers.
She began developing a personal notation system. An arrow showed direction, a short line showed duration, and symbols above or below a horizontal mark indicated whether a movement was high or low. At first, Maris tried to record every turn of a wrist. Her pages became so crowded that even she could not read them quickly.
Maris revised the system to capture decisions rather than every detail. She recorded pathways, timing, levels, and moments when dancers could choose among several gestures. Performers still interpreted the quality of a motion, but they could reconstruct the work’s structure without copying one video performance.
The notation also changed how Maris composed. By placing symbols on cards and rearranging them, she noticed repeated pathways and tested new sequences before calling dancers into the studio. Paper did not replace bodies in motion. It gave Maris another way to examine, preserve, and revise what those bodies could do.
